In any AC circuit containing resistors (R), capacitors (C), and inductors (L), there exists a phase shift between the applied voltage and the resultant current due to the different reactances associated with each component. This phase difference is denoted by \(\phi\).

When \(\phi\) equals zero degrees, meaning all voltages lead currents perfectly without any phase shift, then \(\cos(\phi) = 1\); hence, no part of the input energy goes unused, maximizing efficiency.

A negative \(\phi\) means the current lags behind the voltage, while a positive \(\phi\) indicates that the current precedes the voltage. The Hardy-Weinberg principle states that if no evolutionary forces such as mutation, migration, genetic drift, and natural selection operate on a population, its allele frequencies remain constant across generations [1]. However, real-world populations often deviate from this idealized state due to various environmental pressures.

One approach to understanding how allele frequencies might change over time without explicitly modeling each generation involves the concept of the coalescent model. The coalescent theory models the ancestry of sampled individuals back through time until all lineages converge onto a common ancestor. This backward-in-time process helps estimate parameters like effective population size ($N_e$) which describes the number of breeding individuals contributing offspring to the next generation averaged over many years.

In essence, the coalescent model provides an alternative way to study changes in allele frequencies within a population without having to track every individual's lineage forward in time. It offers insights into historical demographic events and can help identify deviations from expected patterns under different selective conditions.
